newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. could resume wheat export subsidies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. could resume wheat export subsidies.

text.p: Falling U.S. wheat prices in 1997-98 (June-May) could prompt the U.S. Agriculture Department to resume wheat export subsidies for the first time in more than two years, potentially renewing grain trade frictions with Canada.

But whether wheat prices will fall far enough to trigger such subsidies depends on a number of factors, including a possible "El Nino" drought facing the Australian wheat crop, government analysts said.
On Friday, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman reiterated that the United States has the will and "the resources" to match European export subsidies if needed.

"We will fight fire with fire," Glickman told Reuters during a visit to a farm in southeast England. Glickman was in England to speak to the International Grains Council, which held its annual meeting Thursday and Friday.
At first glance, U.S. wheat supplies appear more abundant than in 1994-95, the last full year of USDA wheat export subsidy activity under the Export Enhancement Program.
U.S. wheat ending stocks for 1997-98 are forecast at 579 million bushels, up from 507 million in 1994-95.
WORLD STOCKS AT LOW LEVEL

But world wheat ending stocks are forecast at 115.47 million tonnes, equal to only 20.1 percent of expected use in 1997-98. That's up from 19.0 percent the past two years, but still the third lowest level since at least 1960-61.
Given the tight world supply situation, one private analyst has suggested that the U.S. not use wheat export subsidies as long as it own stocks remain below 800 million bushels.

That viewpoint probably would find support among certain grain exporters and others opposed to the use of export subsidies, said Ed Allen, an international wheat analyst in USDA's Economic Research Service.
But it's not likely to carry much weight with farmers and their representatives in Congress, especially if wheat prices begin sinking, he said.

USDA's current mid-range forecast for 1997-98 U.S. wheat prices is $3.75 per bushel, down from $4.35 in 1996-97 and the record level of $4.55 in 1995-96. Unadjusted for inflation, $3.75 would be the third highest price since 1980-81.

But there's a wide band of uncertainty around that mid-range price forecast. Depending on final 1997-98 U.S. and world wheat production, the actual season-average price could be as low as $3.45 per bushel or as high as $4.05, USDA says.
U.S. CROP LOOKS GOOD

Current prospects for the U.S. wheat crop are better than just a month ago. Good weather during May in the southern Plains helped recoup some of the damage down to the U.S hard red winter crop due to a freeze in April.

Severe flooding in the northern Plains also raised concern about U.S. spring wheat planting. But fields dried out and the crop was "planted in plenty of time," Allen said. Now, there is some concern that conditions are too dry, he added.
Overseas, there "is talk of a record crop in France," Allen said. That increases the chance the EU will resume wheat export subsidies once it gets closer to harvest, he said.

However, wheat plantings in Australia and Argentina are both down from last year. In addition, the presence of an El Nino weather pattern in the Pacific raises the threat of drought to the Australian crop, which won't be harvested until near the end of the year, Allen said.

"If the Australian crop is a bust, Europe may be able to get away" with not subsidizing exports, Allen said. However, the Australian crop generally had favorable moisture at planting, making the impact of El Nino far from certain.

The EU has subsidized wheat exports off and on over the past few years without triggering similar U.S. action. However, if U.S. prices do dip lower, USDA will likely face increased political pressure to match EU action, Allen said.
WHITHER CANADA WHEAT EXPORTS?
Meanwhile, Clinton administration officials continue to warn Canada not to disrupt the U.S. wheat market with a flood of cross-border shipments.

However, an active U.S. export subsidy program could increase those tensions by boosting U.S. wheat prices in comparison to Canadian. That would create more of an incentive for the Canadian Wheat Board, a state trading enterprise for Canada's wheat exports, to sell in the U.S. market.
Current USDA forecasts put Canadian wheat shipments to the U.S. in 1997-98 near the 1.5-million-tonne level that the Clinton administration has said it would tolerate.

That fine balance could be disrupted if the U.S begins subsidizing wheat exports again. In the past, Canadian officials have accused the U.S. Export Enhancement Program (EEP) of creating a price "vacuum" in the U.S. market that pulled Canadian wheat exports down.
The U.S. and Canada will hold talks on grain trade issues on June 27.

Next week, U.S. lawmakers will begin the process of deciding how much funding to provide for EEP in fiscal 1998 (Oct-Sep). The Clinton administration has requested $500 million, but how much Congress will approve remains uncertain.
In February, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that USDA would need just $400 million in fiscal 1998 for EEP.
Market conditions have changed since then, but appropriators are still bound under the congressional budget process to use the $400 million figure as a benchmark for deciding funding levels.

If lawmakers want to use EEP funds for other purposes, they can only claim savings in EEP if they cut the program below $400 million. That could create pressure for an EEP allocation in the range of $300 million, one House aide said.
((Washington commodities desk 202 898 8467))
